prompt: A weather station's daily highs in Celsius have mean $20$ and standard deviation $4$. The data are converted to Fahrenheit using $F = 1.8C + 32$. What is the standard deviation of the Fahrenheit temperatures?
hint: The conversion does two things to each temperature: it multiplies and it adds. Think about which of those changes how spread out the values are.

hints.text: The conversion does two things to each temperature: it multiplies and it adds. Think about which of those changes how spread out the values are.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up with the values $1, 3$, which have SD $\sqrt{2}$. Add $10$ to get $11, 13$ and the SD stays the same. Double them to get $2, 6$ and the SD doubles. Multiplying stretches spread; adding does not.
Adding $32$ shifts every day equally, so it leaves the spread alone. Only the multiplier matters: multiply the Celsius standard deviation $4$ by $1.8$.
$1.8 \times 4 = 7.2$, so the standard deviation is $7.2$ degrees Fahrenheit.

explanation: For a linear change $y = a + bx$, the mean becomes $a + b\bar{x}$ but the standard deviation becomes $|b| \cdot s_x$.
The $+32$ moves every day by the same amount, so the distances between values, and therefore the spread, are untouched.
The multiplier $1.8$ stretches every distance by $1.8$, so $s_F = 1.8 \times 4 = 7.2$ degrees Fahrenheit. (The mean becomes $1.8(20) + 32 = 68$.)

alternativeExplanations.title: Follow two actual days
steps: A day at $20^\circ$C converts to $68^\circ$F. A day one SD warmer, $24^\circ$C, converts to $1.8(24) + 32 = 75.2^\circ$F.
The gap was 4 degrees Celsius and is now $75.2 - 68 = 7.2$ degrees Fahrenheit.
Every gap stretches by 1.8, so the SD does too: 7.2.

alternativeExplanations.title: The trap: adding 32 to the SD
steps: It is tempting to compute $1.8(4) + 32 = 39.2$. That is what happens to the MEAN, not the SD.
Spread measures distances between values, and sliding everything up by 32 leaves every distance alone.
So only the multiplier matters for the SD: $7.2$.
